role: Resident physician, acupuncture department, county hospital of traditional Chinese medicine
headline: An acupuncture resident who did a combined bachelor's and master's at a university of traditional Chinese medicine, spent three years in residency training in the provincial capital, and has just come home to a county TCM hospital in Shandong to spend each day needling a roomful of old people with bad backs and legs
unit: The acupuncture department of the county hospital of traditional Chinese medicine in a farming county in Shandong
education: Master's degree (Acupuncture and Tuina, professional track)
level: You hold both your medical license and your residency certificate, and you can diagnose and needle the common neck, shoulder, back and leg pain and facial palsy on your own. You've only watched acupotomy (needle-knife release) in the provincial hospital and never done it, and you write notes more slowly than you needle
intro: You spent three years of residency training at a top-tier (Grade 3A) TCM hospital in the provincial capital, saw the hardest cases and studied under the best teachers. This year you've come back to the county TCM hospital. The acupuncture department is one treatment room with six beds, and the waiting bench is full of old people holding their backs. As of today they call you the young doctor, and it's your job to get them walking out on their own two feet.
salary_note: Estimate: base pay plus performance pay for a resident at a county TCM hospital in Shandong comes to about ¥5,000 take-home, around sixty percent of the national figure. Housing is cheap and living costs are low in the county, and performance pay follows clinic volume and insurance settlements.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Safe needling on the morning ward round, and handling a patient who faints under the needle

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Body-constitution assessment and seasonal moxibustion plans ahead of each solar term

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 2 related job listings nationwide (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: You ride your e-bike through the county town's morning market. The woman selling jianbing, folded egg pancakes, recognizes you and says her mother-in-law is coming to see you for needles this afternoon.
Department handover. The head runs through the six inpatients: two with the after-effects of stroke, one facial palsy, three herniated lumbar discs. Four of them are yours.

The clinic opens. First is an old man who grows vegetables in greenhouses, bent double, saying he's been squatting in the greenhouse all winter. You have him lie face down and press along the points on his lower back until, at one spot, he lets out a cry.
All six beds are full. You go from bed to bed twirling needles and adjusting the waveform on the electro-acupuncture unit. The smoke from the moxa boxes won't clear, and the extractor fan drones.

An old woman goes white as soon as the needles come out and says everything's going dark. You lay her flat with her head low, give her half a cup of warm sugar water, and stay by the bed until the color comes back to her face.
Twenty minutes' sleep with your head on the desk at lunch, then back to the morning's notes. The hospital system freezes, and you type the four examinations in all over again.

On the ward you needle the man recovering from a stroke to stimulate movement, and today his left hand can close around two of your fingers. His wife wipes her eyes beside the bed. You tell her not to rush; slowly does it.

Home after work, your mother has made a table full of dishes and asks again when you'll meet the person the neighbor wants to introduce. You eat while reading, on your phone, a case your old teacher in the capital has sent.

ladder.title: TCM Resident in Training
ladder.focus: Rotate through the wards of a Grade 3 TCM hospital, building the four examinations and basic needling, moxibustion and cupping, concentrating on medical records and the licensing exam, and passing residency assessment.

ladder.title: Acupuncture Resident Physician
ladder.focus: Work as the department's front-line doctor on call, managing beds on the acupuncture ward, treating at the bedside and answering emergency consults on your own, and handling needling accidents and combined electro-acupuncture plans.

ladder.title: Acupuncture Attending Physician
ladder.focus: Run your own specialist acupuncture clinic focused on one or two conditions, such as facial nerve palsy or stubborn neck and back pain, train residents, and start working on the department's research projects.

ladder.title: Associate Chief Physician of Acupuncture
ladder.focus: Lead consultations on difficult and severe cases, practice minimally invasive techniques such as acupotomy, lead provincial or national research projects, and build a regional reputation.

ladder.title: Chief Physician of Acupuncture
ladder.focus: Shape the discipline, write clinical guidelines for specialist conditions, supervise graduate students and disciples, and either share in the fees of a premium expert clinic or lead the department's discipline.

ai_tasks.name: Safe needling on the morning ward round, and handling a patient who faints under the needle
ai_tasks.how: Inserting the needle, judging the arrival of qi, positioning the patient and preventing fainting all happen at the bedside, by touch and close watching; AI can't do any of it. At most AI tidies up a first draft of the progress note for the doctor to check and sign.

ai_tasks.name: Morning needling on the ward and emergency handling of needle fainting
ai_tasks.how: Needling high-risk points, checking retained needles and rescuing a patient within thirty seconds are hands-on, accountable work for doctors and nurses only. AI can at most help draft the paperwork for the doctor to revise.

ai_tasks.name: Body-constitution assessment and seasonal moxibustion plans ahead of each solar term
ai_tasks.how: AI helps gather the four examinations, read infrared thermal images and draft seasonal moxibustion or herbal-plaster plans. The doctor rechecks the constitution face to face and finalizes the plan with contraindications and the patient's wishes in mind.

ai_tasks.name: A stroke patient's first acupuncture session to stimulate movement, with motor evoked potential monitoring started at the same time
ai_tasks.how: The equipment records the MEP baseline and organizes the data, and AI can flag anomalies. The doctor chooses the points and technique, judges what the patient can tolerate, and keeps it safe.

ai_tasks.name: Precise localization and risk assessment before acupotomy release for a patient referred from a township clinic
ai_tasks.how: AI helps mark pain points on the images, outline nerves and vessels and suggest a route. The doctor confirms the plan by touch and experience, and the procedure itself and the risk decisions rest with a person.

ai_tasks.name: Handling a needle-fainting incident from start to finish, and the root-cause analysis afterward
ai_tasks.how: The rescue on the spot has to be done by people. Afterward AI can sort the records, the procedure log and the timeline and draft the root-cause report, and the medical team verifies the cause and sets the fixes.

ai_tasks.name: Virtual point location and home moxibustion monitoring during remote acupuncture guidance on the hospital's online clinic
ai_tasks.how: AI uses image recognition to judge whether a point is off and whether moxibustion is being done properly, and reminds the patient in real time. The doctor handles anything unusual, watches for burns and other risks, and decides on changes to the plan.

events.e_sanfu: The first of the Dog Days, the hottest stretch of summer, when people come for herbal plasters on their backs. The line in the hospital courtyard ran from six in the morning to noon. You put plasters on more than two hundred backs before lunch, and your fingers were stained yellow.
events.e_facial: A middle-school boy came in with facial palsy, the corner of his mouth drooping, too ashamed to go to school. In the third week of needling he puffed out his cheeks in the mirror and not a breath leaked out. His mother cried in the doorway of the treatment room.
events.e_faint: An old man who'd come in on an empty stomach fainted with the needles in. Needles out, flat on his back, press the point under the nose, call the nurse: in thirty seconds you did what you'd drilled countless times in training. The first thing he said when he came round was: Doctor, I hadn't had breakfast.
events.e_eggs: An old woman whose back you'd fixed came on market day with a basket of eggs from her own hens, set it down and left before you could catch her. The department rule is no gifts, so you slipped the money into her grandson's school bag.
events.e_doubt: A young man home from migrant work elsewhere had two sessions, said they did nothing, and posted online that acupuncture is all in the mind. The department head read it and told you not to reply; just needle him properly next time.
events.e_match: The person the neighbor introduced teaches at the county's No. 1 high school. You met at a new café in town, and they said an old relative at home had been to you for needles, and their back was much better. Afterward the two of you often walked along the river embankment.
events.e_moxa_smoke: In winter there were so many moxibustion patients that the smoke couldn't clear from the room, and you were hoarse for two weeks. When the department finally got a new extraction system, you were the first to sign off on it.
events.e_dip: Medical insurance changed how it pays, and acupuncture was capped at a few body areas per session; anything over isn't reimbursed. You explained to a patient why it could only be three sessions this week, and he slammed the door on his way out.
events.e_township: The county set up a joint health network, and every Wednesday you went out to see patients at the township clinic. The consulting room was a converted storeroom, the radiator barely warm, and more old people came than in town.
events.e_wedding: You held the wedding at a hotel in the county town, thirty tables, half of them patients you'd needled and their families. The emcee said it was the oldest crowd he'd ever hosted.
events.e_classmate: A classmate from residency stayed at the top-tier hospital in the capital and posted that they'd done their first acupotomy, the operating lights blinding. You liked the post, turned your phone face down on the desk, and went back to your notes.
events.e_house: You bought a three-bedroom flat in the county's new district, a ¥200,000 down payment, not too hard. From the balcony you can see the hospital.
events.e_stroke: The stroke patient you'd looked after for three months walked to the lift on his own crutches the day he was discharged. He turned and waved to you, and his fingers opened.
events.e_baby: The day your child was born, you waited outside the delivery room, pressing without thinking on the Neiguan point on your own wrist.
events.e_video: You filmed a short video outside the department on “three points for back pain from sitting too long.” A nurse posted it on a whim, and it gained twenty thousand followers in a week. Some of the people booking appointments started saying they'd seen the video.
events.e_ai_tizhi: The hospital bought an AI constitution analyzer. Patients put a hand on it and stick out their tongue at the camera, and two minutes later a report comes out. Your day gained one more task: checking whether it's right, then taking the pulse yourself.
events.e_master: The legacy studio of a renowned senior TCM doctor in the province took on students from county hospitals, and you were chosen. Two days a month you sat in on his clinic in the capital. He barely spoke while he needled, and you sketched his hand positions in your notebook.
events.e_remote: The hospital opened an online clinic, and you coached patients in other towns through home moxibustion on a phone screen, with AI checking whether they'd found the right points. One old man held the moxa stick too close, and you called out from your side of the screen.
events.e_neck: Years of bending to insert and twirl needles, and your neck was the first to go. You put a few needles in yourself, and they didn't work as well as they do on other people.
events.e_paper: Associate chief physician requires papers and research projects, and the county has no laboratory. You pulled out the records of three hundred-odd back-pain patients from these years one by one, and typed statistics tables at home in the evenings.
events.e_trainee: You started supervising residents. Watching one's hand shake on his first needle, you remembered practicing finger strength on paper pads, and pushed a stack of them across to him.
events.e_father: Your father farmed all his life, and his back is more bent than any of your patients'. At the weekend you went back to the village to needle him. Lying face down on the heated brick bed, he said: never thought it'd end up being you putting needles in me.
events.e_young_leave: The department advertised for three years and only one person ever reported for work, and after a year they left for the capital too. Before the old department head retired, he took your arm and said the acupuncture department was up to you now.

c_attending.title: Sit the Acupuncture Attending Physician exam
c_attending.situation: Once you've served enough years as a resident you can sit the attending physician exam in TCM acupuncture, and only then can you run a specialist clinic on your own. But the department is short-handed, you're on clinic and ward all day, and the only time to study is at night.

options.label: Study at night, sit it this year
options.result: You studied until one every night, and the pages smelled of moxa smoke. The day the results came out you needled thirty patients in a row in clinic and never got a chance to look at your phone.

options.label: Get solid in clinic first
options.result: You saw a few hundred more patients and your technique got steadier. The exam was pushed back a year, and a classmate who'd come back the same year got the certificate first.

c_jinxiu.title: Six months' training in acupotomy in the capital
c_jinxiu.situation: The hospital has one place for advanced training at a top-tier hospital in the capital, learning ultrasound-guided acupotomy, which would let you start a new service back home. Training pays base salary only for six months, and someone has to hold the fort at home.

options.label: Go for the training
options.result: In the capital you did dozens of cases under your teacher, and for the first time saw clearly on ultrasound the needle tip touching the fascia. When you came back, the department hung a sign for the new service.

options.label: Give the place to a colleague
options.result: Your colleague went and came back as the department's first acupotomy doctor. Patients ask for him by name, and you keep using your filiform needles.

c_province.title: Apply to the top-tier TCM hospital in the capital
c_province.situation: The capital hospital where you trained is hiring acupuncture doctors, and your old teacher calls to say you should try. It's a bigger stage with more research, but you'd start at the back of the line again, rent a flat, and either move the family or live apart.

options.label: Go back to the capital
options.result: You got the job and started again from the bottom in the capital. Your patients changed from old people with bad backs to difficult cases from all over the province.

options.label: Stay in the county
options.result: You stayed. The county patients are the same old people with bad backs and legs, more every year, and some have started calling you the old doctor.

c_video.title: Take short health videos seriously, or not
c_video.situation: The hospital's publicity office wants you to open an account and film two videos a week on seasonal health and acupressure points. Some say it's just drumming up business for the hospital; others say doctors shouldn't perform for the internet. Filming would eat your lunch breaks and weekends.

options.label: Film them, and do it properly
options.result: Your account grew to over a hundred thousand followers in a year, and people from other counties rode two hours to book you. One video was cut into an ad for moxa patches, and you spent two weeks filing complaints.

options.label: Don't, just see patients
options.result: You said no. Your appointments are as hard to get as ever, and new patients are the ones old patients bring along.

c_ai.title: Learn AI assessment and remote care, or not
c_ai.situation: The province has given county hospitals an AI constitution-assessment system and remote moxibustion guidance, and needs a doctor to lead it: checking the AI's diagnoses, setting the remote plans, and writing into the protocol who answers for a burn. The old department head says the machine can see a tongue, but not what's on someone's mind.

options.label: Lead it, learn to manage it
options.result: You compared the system's assessments with your own diagnoses one by one and wrote down where it went wrong. Six months on, you can tell at a glance which lines of its reports to trust.

options.label: Stay out, keep to the pulse
options.result: You still take the pulse with three fingers and place needles one at a time. The young doctors run reports on the system, and when they're not sure, they come and ask you.

c_overseas.title: Go abroad to practice acupuncture
c_overseas.situation: A university classmate runs an acupuncture clinic abroad and says that with a local license you can practice there and earn several times what you make now. You'd have to pass an English exam and the licensing exam, move the family, and leave your parents in the county.

options.label: Get licensed and go
options.result: It took you two years to earn an overseas acupuncture license.
options.end: You needle people in a city that speaks another language. Patients can't say your name right, but their bad backs are exactly like those old people's back in the county.

options.label: Stay
options.result: You said your parents are here, and so are your patients. Your classmate sent a postcard, and you pinned it to the treatment-room wall.

c_vice.title: Apply for Associate Chief Physician of Acupuncture
c_vice.situation: Associate chief physician needs papers, research projects and years of rural service, which are hard to put together in a county. Your teacher in the capital will take you onto a project, but that means two years of weekends given to statistics tables and literature.

options.label: Apply, and do the research
options.result: You switched back and forth between clinic and spreadsheets, and lost a fair bit of hair. At your defense a judge asked about a case, and you even named the patient's village.

options.label: Don't apply, just see patients
options.result: You didn't apply. Your clinic is still booked into next week, and one patient said: Doctor, that “associate” doesn't matter.

c_private.title: Open a TCM clinic with a partner
c_private.situation: An old patient who trades in medicinal herbs wants to open a TCM clinic in the county town and asks you to be his partner, seeing patients and running the medical side, for double your income. Leaving the public hospital means giving up your permanent state post and your professional title.

options.label: Leave and open the clinic
options.result: You handed in your resignation. The department head didn't try to keep you; he just said come back and visit.
options.end: You opened a TCM clinic at the corner of the old street in the county town, with a sign you lettered yourself. The patients are the same old people holding their backs, and some followed you all the way from the hospital.

options.label: Stay at the hospital
options.result: You turned him down. He hired someone else for the clinic, and it does well. Now and then you pass it and see the lights on late.

c_director.title: Go for Chief Physician of Acupuncture and take over the department
c_director.situation: The old department head is retiring and the hospital wants you to take over: apply for chief physician, manage a dozen staff, and push for the county's key specialty status. Take all that on, and your clinic hours get cut in half.

options.label: Take over the department
options.result: You started writing specialty-development reports, drawing up rotas and going back and forth to the county health commission. One day you realized you hadn't touched a needle in a week.

options.label: Just see patients
options.result: You let a slightly younger colleague take the department and stayed in the treatment room. Those six beds are still the ones you know best.

endings.retire: At your last clinic you take the needles out of an old patient you've treated for more than ten years and help her button her padded coat. She asks who she'll see when you've gone. You say the young doctor I trained, whose hands are steadier than mine. You give your needle case to the nurse, take off your white coat and hang it on the back of the door.
endings.burnout: That winter your neck and your back gave out together, and the hand that twirls the needles began to go numb. The hospital moved you to the preventive medicine center, to see patients without needling them. You leave on time every day, and when you pass the acupuncture department you still glance in to see who's lying on those few beds.

past: The year you were in your first year at the county's No. 1 high school, your grandfather had a stroke and lost the use of half his body. An old TCM doctor from the township came to the house every day to needle him, and six months later your grandfather could hold chopsticks on his own. You watched from beside the bed the whole six months.

After the gaokao (college entrance exam) you chose Acupuncture and Tuina at the university of TCM in the provincial capital, a five-year degree. Your father said traditional medicine was a good choice: the older you get, the more you're worth.

In your second year, memorizing the meridians and points, you traced them on your own legs, and your roommates took turns being your model. The point you needled most was Zusanli, just below the knee.

After your bachelor's you got into the professional master's in Acupuncture and Tuina, with graduate study and residency training combined: rotating through the departments of a top-tier hospital by day, writing your thesis at night.
You passed the national TCM medical licensing exam. That year you handled a patient fainting under the needle on the ward on your own for the first time, and your hands shook for an hour afterward.

You finished residency and your master's together. The hospital in the capital offered a chance to stay, but you'd have to wait for a permanent post; the director of the county TCM hospital called you himself to say the old head of acupuncture was about to retire. You went back to the county.

late.pension_note: Estimate: doctors with a permanent post at a county TCM hospital are in the public-institution pension scheme, and with the occupational annuity, the pension comes to a little over sixty percent of your final monthly pay.
scenes: For the first month of retirement you still woke at seven-thirty and went for a turn round the morning market. The jianbing seller asked why you weren't at work today, and you said you'd stopped.
The hospital rehired you for two half-day clinics a week, and the appointment board says “Senior Expert.” You looked at it and found it a little funny.
In the Dog Days you went back to the hospital courtyard to help put on the summer plasters. In the line was that boy with facial palsy, grown up and holding a child of his own.
A meridian chart hangs on your study wall, bought during residency, its corners curled. A grandchild points at the little dots and asks what they are, and you read them out one by one.
At the preventive medicine center you talk to people about the solar terms, what to eat and how to sleep: all the things you never managed to do yourself.
Your neck slowly mended, and now and then you could needle your family again. Your mother, lying on the bed, said yours still don't hurt.
When the time came you retired, and every Thursday afternoon you teach acupressure to your old neighbors on the estate, free. More come than you expected.
In the first year away from the county hospital you kept waking at seven-thirty, and only then remembered there was no handover to go to.
You found your feet in the new place. Now and then an old patient from the county tracks you down, saying they only trust your needles. You treat them and don't charge.
A resident you trained went back to the county hospital as head of department and sent you a photo of the new ward: the six beds have become twenty.

Later AI could read a tongue coating and find the points, and even warn you when moxa was too hot. But the feel of the needle going in, and the patient saying “that's the spot,” still needed a person at the bedside.
There's a thin callus on the thumb and forefinger of your right hand, from decades of twirling needles. On rainy days it stiffens a little, and you press your own Hegu point, in the web of the hand.

closing.retire: Many years later, on a morning in the Dog Days, you pass the hospital and see the long line back in the courtyard, young doctors putting plasters on old people. You stand in the shade of a tree and watch for a while. You don't go in. You walk slowly home.
closing.burnout: Many years later you dry mugwort on the balcony, leaves you cut yourself on the river embankment. The sun is good, the leaves are silvery grey on the underside, and the whole flat is full of that familiar smell.
closing.end: Many years later, at the bottom of a trunk, you find a box of needles from your residency, your name written on the lid in ballpoint, faded now. You open it and look, then gently close it.

stages: You are the department's front line. Every day you manage four or five beds: morning rounds and progress notes, then needling ward patients and adjusting the electro-acupuncture units in the afternoon. On call, when the emergency department asks for a consult, you're the first one down the stairs. The department head sets the plan and you carry it out; when you're unsure of a point combination, you write it up in the records system and ask the head to look first.

You have your own specialist clinic now, for neck and back pain and facial palsy. Diagnosis, point selection and technique are all your call, and residents needle to the plans you write; your signature in the records system is the final word on each case. You've started supervising residents and running the department's case discussions, and now and then the hospital sends you to give a health talk.

The difficult cases start coming to you: foot drop after a stroke, backs that still hurt after surgery. You do ultrasound-guided acupotomy, write opinions on consult forms, and run the data for a county research project; when doctors at the township clinics in the network call to ask about a plan, you talk them through it point by point.

The whole acupuncture department is yours. Once a week you run the department meeting: rotas, insurance settlement sheets, clinical protocols for specialist conditions. You still keep a premium clinic, and its appointments are gone the moment they're released. The residents you trained are spread across the townships, and often call to tell you about a patient. When they finish, you say: bring them in tomorrow and I'll take a look.
work: At eleven at night the emergency department calls a consult: a truck driver with a crick in his neck who can't turn his head. You put one needle in the stiff-neck point on the back of his hand and tell him to turn slowly. He turns.
The head nurse comes round with the needling skills checklist for a spot test. You locate twenty points on the training model and get one wrong, and she circles it on the sheet.
In the records system you write a facial-palsy patient's first progress note, half a page on the four examinations. The department head changes only one term: “wind-cold” to “wind-heat.”
A new resident needling Huantiao, deep in the hip, stops halfway and is afraid to go further. You take hold of his hand and let him feel the resistance of the layer under the needle tip.

Someone from the hospital's insurance office brings a stack of settlement sheets: a dozen patients last month went over the cap on body areas. You go through the records one by one and write the reasons on the back of each sheet.

On the county TV station's solar-term program you talk about moxibustion at the winter solstice. The host asks you to find Zusanli on her leg; you find it at the first try, and she says it aches a little.
A township clinic doctor shows you an old man's lumbar MRI on a video call. You circle two segments and tell him to bring the films into town tomorrow.

Watching the needle tip slide along the fascia on the ultrasound screen, you release the back of a carpenter who still hurt after surgery. He gets off the table, takes two steps, and says his leg feels lighter.
The project statistician sends a data sheet: of three hundred cases, twenty are missing follow-up. You phone each one, and get seventeen back.

The hospital director brings the application for the county's key specialty status. On the review form you rewrite the clinical protocol three times, and the final version adds a referral pathway from the townships.
At the department meeting you put next quarter's insurance settlement data on the screen and go through it line by line: which patients need costs controlled, and which can't lose a single needle.

A graduate student you supervise brings the thesis proposal for your signature. On page three you say: the sham acupuncture for the control group, think again about how to do it without deceiving anyone.
